Topics discussed are the Platt Cattle Ranching Operations centered on the Salmon River Rangeland with support from their farm Genesee, the settlement and strategic location of early Genesee and wheat raising in the area, and the livery business and annual horse show on rodeo in the town.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the town like there when you were just a kid?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Every business house was filled up. Every place along the line had something in it. My dad ran a livery stable there and that was just about the east end of town as far as any business was concerned. But across from us was a creamery. Up the line a couple of little ways was a hardware store, furniture store, and then just keep right on going through town. Every place was filled up. Everything was lively. And there were two or three blacksmith shops later. Later, of course, some of those turned, a couple of them turned into garages, but at that time why they were blacksmith shops for shoeing horses and fixing farm equipment. And I don't have any idea how many places there were that were actually places of business, but I can remember when there were a couple of grocery stores and two or three, two merchandise stores. There's mercantile stores where they handle dry goods and this type of thing. And my recollection of the thing I like to remember about it is that where we lived down on the flat was right in the area where they had the old ball field one time. And the city ball field was right close there, but it was also the place where the Indians came when the Indians moved into town or came in for a celebration while they came down and stayed right down on that flat close to us. And they would go back and forth, of course, from town. And it seemed like the recollections that I have mostly of Genesee is the old horse years. Three days of horse show every spring and usually two days of rain. So they were always assured of a good crop. They had lots of big horses, lots of draft horses and lots of, well not lots, but quite a few head of herefords and big cattle of some kind there that they were raising. And lots of big old Perch and horse, Perch and Belgian shire horses. And of course, there at the livery stable, there was always two or three stud horses that were standing there during the season to take care of the mares. But I can remember those, especially those horse shows, because they were always assured of at least two days of rain out of the three. It was in June.

speaker: Sam Schrager

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is that right?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, yes.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was three days of the horse show and rodeo. It was a horse show and rodeo combined. I can remember one time of old Sundown Jackson in Nez Perce Indian that was world champion rider being there at the fair. And he gave me the job of, I was just a kid around the livery stable, but he gave me the job of exercising his horse for him. And I took the horse out for a little ride in the morning. Then that afternoon, why he would take the horse and ear him down and put a hack-a-more on him and throw the saddle on him and that thing would just buck and balls. You'd think he was an outlaw, but he was just as tame as could be if he wanted him. Then after it was all over, he'd put the saddle back on him and away they'd go again.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I would imagine that all the staff that came up this street were registered. Oh yes, sure they were. They were real good for all the animals. speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And they knew about it too.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh yes, there's no question about it because it was the only real event that they had at that time. And as Tom says, the Indians made up a good share of the show because they were in the parade and taking part. And then they took part in the rodeo too, some of them, the ones that wanted to.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Could you describe what you remember about your father's livery? The blacksmith in operation there? What he did?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, he had a livery stable, but not blacksmiths. No, there were at least two blacksmiths in town at the time, but he didn't have one. The earliest memory I have of it was probably after it was going downhill a little bit because I only remember him having about 12 or 14 horses. That is six or eight teams, six teams or seven teams. And they had teams that were hired out for people to drive and then other teams that they furnished drivers with. And at one time, this was in the early days, Genesee was the end of the railroad, long before the railroad got into Moscow. And so anyone wanting to go to Lewiston came to Genesee and then worked the town there and the dry goods part of it, the dry goods salesman. And then they took a hack and went from there on down to Lewiston. And this was the regular run every so often for the livery stable to take two or three drummers down to Lewiston with their suitcases and sample bags and so forth. And it was only about 20 miles, so this wasn't so awfully far travel. And later, oh about 1914, 15, somewhere along there, Dad had a couple of automobiles. 1912 Velie and 1913 Rio and ran a taxi service then for the next three or four years. And I'm not just sure which year it was or where it comes in, but oh about 1917, 18, somewhere along about wartime was when Dad went to work for Tom and Kenny's dad, the Padaleck brothers. And then he farmed for them for a couple of years and then went out on his own later and bought a farming outfit. But that was the end of the livery stable anyway, about the first of the World War.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that it had to do with the change in automobiles that made him decide to work those visions?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I'm sure this was part of it. Of course at that time there was, in the early days there were no roads. There still weren't any roads in 1915, 16, there were still all dirt roads except that one stretch of road east of Genesee which had been put in oh somewhere around 1910 probably. They had put in a mile or a mile or a little over a rock road there. And this was the only rock road in the country. The rest of it was all dirt. So automobiles weren't very popular in the wintertime for quite some time. And eventually they would be able to get gravel roads in the country.

words: Would you happen to know that day before they rocked the streets in Genesee, before they rocked that road which came from?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt

One of the things I remember a long time back is a fellow named Morgan who was the head of the telephone company in there. He lived way up on the north hill and he would drive in with this old car he has. I don't even remember what make it was. Two or three cylinder car. Two cylinder maybe. And he'd get just about 50 yards up this first hill if it was at least a bit slick. Well, that's as far as he ever went. Then he'd go home and get a pair of mules and take the car on home. But now, I don't know why, at that time he always went up that hill there by the old Herman furniture store. speaker: Sam Schrager

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Dad had his phone there in the barn so it had to have been in there after 1910, 12, somewhere along there that they put it in. See, Genesee was only three miles actually from the first Indian reservation, the north boundary of the reservation. words: The land right around Genesee, all the land that we still have there, the Hickman family still have, was Platt Brothers at one time or was Platt's. speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well that's when Mother was born, was in 81. But at that time the land around Genesee was all taken up, so they had to buy land. They could have come on farther up toward Moscow Mountain here and got land, but around Genesee it was all taken up at that time.

words: Do you have an idea of why they picked that place, why Genesee wanted? Well, the story was that they came to Uniontown and stayed with a sister, wasn't that it?

words: Well, he started working on orchards down on the Snake River and worked on ranch there for a year or two before he finally bought this livery stable. But he worked there a little while anyway on some of these farms.

words: Well, when Mr. Platt came in 81, the land was owned.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know how developed it was though? Was it very much under the plow already? I mean, wasn't much of it producing crop?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I would doubt that. They had no great place to send a crop. No one could get rid of it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They had to take it to all of us. They had to feed it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They had to feed the pigs and drive the pigs somewhere. Or hey, they had to feed the cattle or horses or something of that sort. And there's another factor in there. There's been a big climate change because it was years before they could raise wheat on the Genesee class.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: 1917. The first war. It just about started. Yeah, it was during the first war they started.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Before that, at the time we were talking about, beyond back the time we were talking about, talking about in the 1880s, those flats were Timothy and Clover. Hay. Of course, there was a big demand for hay then. All this work was horses. All transportation was horses. Unless it was even slower with oxen. So the whole climate has changed. And we have some pictures around some place. One of them, I think, is with your dad. And it's taken in front of Paul's store. And you can just see his head over the snow banks where they shoveled snow off.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That was 1912 or 13 when they tunneled through in order to get back and forth on one side of the street the other.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I don't know. You see, there's been a tremendous change. So stock was much more important in the early days than it was after the war. And it continued to be important for a long time because they drove stock from over around Grangeville. They even drove hogs from over in there, cottonwood in Grangeville, to Genesee because Genesee was the end of the railroad. They knew where they could go. That's what made Genesee for a long time.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: During the war, they came in there with the horses for the French cavalry before we got mixed up in the war. They brought those salmon river and Grangeville and over in that country. Brought them across the Indian Reservation and probably picked up a pony or two as they came along. Anyway, they sold them out then. And the idea there was that they had to ride them through the gate in order to show that they were broken. Some of them hadn't even had to saddle on them before. But then they rode them through the gate anyway. I can remember that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who grew them? Who raised the horses?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, they came off the salmon river. I'm not even sure where the horses came from in the first place. But they came off the salmon river breaks down there someplace. Somebody was in the horse business.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Just about everybody over there had a few horses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It's funny because now you're thinking that it's so completely farming country. You don't think of it as much as being horse country. You know that is so much of it's stock country.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But if every farmland or every piece of land, say 160 acres, had to have... Well, we had eight or ten horses there when we farmed that 160 there at home, 170 acres. If every piece of land had that many horses, there was an enormous amount of that land that was going right back into feed and grain to feed those horses. And well, the captain and Driscoll out there with their big outfit they had, and they had a bunch of mules.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Thirty, forty mules around.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know how many mules they would have to farm a layout like they had, but it was a good many of them. Took seven horses usually on a gang plow, two bottom plow. Now they start out with an eight or six or eight bottom plow behind one of these tractors.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the marketing problems? Do you remember much about what that was like or what they used to say it was like in the early days?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, when you got beyond the point where you had transportation and could sell grain and stuff like that for cash, well it was the same as it is today as far as I know. And of course the big packing companies were not long in establishing packing houses at Spokane, Seattle, and ..., Frye.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: You can remember Tom Mowen when they had hay warehouse there at Genesee. Sure, I remember going there. They had apple packing house there. They had, one time, I don't remember it necessarily, but they must have had prune dryers because there were prune orchards scattered all over that area.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Did the Genesee slaughterhouse slaughter for out shipments or just local? That was still operating?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, in my time, old ... and Raiders and so forth, they were just doing their own butchering or butchering for people, local people. I don't know that they were butchering for anybody out of town at all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well I was thinking more about the time back before 1900 even, I mean those really early years when you were saying there wasn't much to market. I would imagine that there would be a lot of difficulty for...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well Tom mentioned driving pigs now. I can't imagine driving pigs, but this was one of Millard's dad's stories that he used to tell how they used to raise pigs out here in this Lenville country where they lived, the Armstrongs. And then when they got them ready for market, they'd drive them to Colfax, cross country. Well I can't imagine driving pigs, but that's...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It don't seem possible, but I guess they did it. I know my dad mentioned the first time he saw old birds, they were coming over to the prairie with a drive of pigs I think.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was it like getting down to Lewiston from Genesee in the early days? What was it like to get down? Was that grade pretty tough?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well the grades had been improved time after time, but the old Central grade, and there was a grade that came up through by Archibald's, came off that Central grade. And then the old Union town grade was...they've been there for, well I guess ever since they've been people up on these hills because they... Just here a while back they made this Collins place, a historical site, the house and the granary, and that was right on the old stage road. And then of course there was another stage road that came out of Lewiston and came up through Genesee when Genesee was down at the old town. And went right on through past the fort and came up through Moscow and Farmington, I believe Farmington was the end of the route. And then they turned around there and went on back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: If you were trading, would you be more likely to trade Lewiston or Moscow in Genesee?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well I don't know. I would suspect that at that time you'd have to stay in Genesee because I think they had the transportation and the goods and the stores.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So I realized, I was thinking of the bigger, if you had to go to a big town, which was a town that Genesee felt would feel closer to as far as that sort of purchasing.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Gee, I don't know.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I would imagine Lewiston, because Lewiston in those days was what they called a seaport. They were bringing boats in there in the early days. In fact they tell the story that when they were building later, building that railroad up the river, the Orofino up in there, that one railroad ran a boat with a high mast up through there and made it put in draw bridges all the way to Kooskia. While the other railroad was building in there. So that whole area is draw bridges. But they knocked the bottom out of the boat every time they went up and back. That didn't matter. I don't know, like Tom says, they were pretty well self-supporting, but I've heard them old timers tell, and Mildred's dad was one of them, about going to Palouse to get their flower ground, because there was a flower mill at Palouse. Of course I imagine there was a flower mill in, oh maybe in Colfax or maybe Lewiston and some of these other towns all this time too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So they'd have to go that far to...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They'd go over one day and get their wheat ground and then lay over a day and then bring it home the next day. Or just trade it for wheat, I don't know which they would do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's pretty interesting because I know that of course people in the northern end of the county went to Palouse, but I had no idea that its draw was so big, taking people from all the way down to Genesee.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you guys know your grandfather Flat? Was he still alive? What do you remember about him?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I even remember great grandfather Harris, but mostly what I can remember about him is the old corn cake that he used to smoke in that pipe of his.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I remember him better than grandfather Plath. He was in that little house back in the church there when I lived with grandmother in the school there. I mean we used to go over there quite a bit.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: He came over. Well, grandpa Plath apparently was quite a public minded citizen because he was mixed up in quite a few things to help him promote the community. But this great grandfather we talk about Harris, he was an old minister, Methodist minister and retired at the time Tom and I knew him. He married my dad and mother in 98 and then was retired of course when I knew him. But he used to come down every Sunday or almost every Sunday and have dinner with us down at the house and sit on the back porch and watch the ball game and smoke his corn cob pipe and give the folks the fits for playing ball on Sunday. But he didn't miss a day anyway to come down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He'd been in Genesee then as a minister in the real early days?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: He was a minister at Leland when he married dad and mother. He came from England. But no, I don't know that he ever was a minister in Genesee.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well he didn't come even until after grandfather and grandma were settled there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, that's right. He wasn't one of the real early ones. He came later anyway.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you remember about the farm when you were a kid growing up there? Did your father have much going by then? Pretty big operation?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well pretty sizable, yes. In most parts I remember about it in work. No, he had one big ranch.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They farmed that ranch there in town, 170 acres or so. Then they rented a little more around there. Then they had 700 acres out on that fallout place plus the canyon, which was another 700 acres or so. That all was farmed with horses. Besides Tom's folks there, or Tom and Kenny's folks both, had at least 200 head of purebred Herefords that were kept there on the place in town. Well I say they were kept there. They were later when they got the fallout place while they were running the canyons too, some of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know about when they started bringing in the purebred stock?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I would think it was the spring of 1915.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: 14th of November. It could be. It was just before the start of the war I imagine.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I suspect that he brought the first full Hereford cattle to Idaho. I don't know of any others.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you know about how he brought them in? Where he got them from and how he got them?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: He got them in Iowa, Iowa and Nebraska. He just went back there and picked out what he wanted and bought them. I guess I should have put it another way. He picked out what he could afford and shipped them out here.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And later some of them came from Kansas City when they went to that, took a bunch of stock back to that show back there and came back with a bigger carload than they took back in the first place.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, he went back that other time and was getting so many calls for bulls he couldn't begin to supply it and they went back there and bought a carload of young bulls shipped out here and brought Archie Kane along with them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Archie Kane was a?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: A herdsman. He was a herdsman for some time.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: See by that time they were putting out a show herd and they didn't do good herdsmen.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know what made your father decide to go from his earlier operation into purebred?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, I don't really. Maybe he just wanted into it. It probably seemed like a good investment at the time. I guess probably it was. Things broke along.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well they always told me, both John and Bill, two brothers, that they owed about $125 ,000 to Outfit that was investing in livestock. You know, it was a livestock organization that loaned money and they had offered to pay it up time and again but this Outfit was never interested in being paid up. It was just a good investment for them to leave it there and take the interest on it. Well then when things began to get tough and they really got out to the place where the boys were getting pinched a bit, then this Outfit stepped in and said, well we have to have our money. And when they did, well that was practically the end of it. I can remember purebred Herefords being sold for $32 a head right at the end of the depression or right at the start of the depression. Of course they certainly couldn't come out on anything like that. But...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well from the beginning of the purebred operation, about how many did he start with, you know?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: About what size it was.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Do you remember how many stanchions there was on each side of the whole barn there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, I don't. I would suppose 20 on each side probably.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Was there that many?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I know the winter of 17. After I got out of the hospital with Typhoid, they went up there and helped feed them and they put the cows all in. I can remember there was 12 in that old barn that's where the new horse barn was. And we put the rest of them in the stanchions on the two sides of the old barn and we had everything covered. That was the extent of the cow herd.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: 45, 50 head at the most.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So I would say that he brought a car load and those were cattle that you tied up in the car. So probably he started with around 25 head of cows and heifers.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But one winter there when we worked at the...dad and I hauled straw, and that's practically the only thing we did that winter, was break the trail out of there to haul straw with four horses for bedding. And I'm sure that at that time they had about 200 head of purebreds. So that kept building up anyway, where they had quite a few head.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember how many years later that would have been?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, that wouldn't have been...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was early 20s?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I wasn't even going to say it was that far along. Maybe it was 19, but in 1921 or 22, dad was farming the fallow place. He was out there. So it was before that time. So it might have been just about in 1920.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he find much demand for the stock once he started getting going with it?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, while it's a thing that goes up and down, when cattle are high, there is a big demand for good bulls because people are stocking up for cattle. When they go down and people begin to sell off, then your market begins to drop on them too. So it's an up and down roller coaster sort of a thing, really. I don't know how you get away from that. It seems to just go through all the stock.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that his bringing in the purebreds had a much better effect on the stock growing in the area? I mean, do you think people started getting a lot more interested in this type of real good breed of animal?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, the stockman, if he's any good, is always looking to better himself. He knows that when he betters his cattle, he betters himself. So yes, I think that he could be looking to improve.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This would be like when you said the demand for bulls. That would be that kind of thing. Sure.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Of course, you have to remember, too, that these two fellows had, oh, what, 1100 head of range stock on Salmon River. They took some bulls for that to keep that outfit going. They owned that much, you see, besides a couple bands of sheep.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Actually, the demand for purebred bulls was not in the Genesee community. It was in the outlying range areas where range cattle were produced. As far as I know, my father and uncle were the only purebred preferred producers in the Genesee area. And they didn't sell many to other farmers and so on in that area. Their sales were farther away.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: A few out on the breaks, people that had pasture, like Clearwater Ranch, the Swingys, and some of those people that had a lot of canyon pasture out there, gave them a lot more.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I think you could say that the whole development of Genesee related to other areas pretty much throughout its history. When our grandparents came there, as Dave has said, the land was already taken up. They had to buy land. They couldn't homestead. And when my father got old enough to start doing stuff on his own, there was not an opportunity to go into farming in the Genesee area without buying land or renting. So our grandfather sent him off to San Bernardino to start a ranch business. And there was, for many years, a kind of a neutral benefit relationship between production of purebred breeding stock in Genesee and the use of that stock on the range areas. And because this was before the time of bottom of the Oats, there was quite a bit of refinement in the use of horses. As Dave mentioned, his dad ran a livery stable, but he didn't do freight hauling. Well, in town, the local hauling was done by people in the drain business.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This was a drain.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was going farther. It was freeing.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So there was really specialization. Oh yeah. In those days, every grocery store made deliveries around town. They would have their own cart or their own rig, or else they rented it from a drain outlet to do their delivering for them. And this was a big business to haul everything around to the people that they bought. Maybe just a little bit of groceries, but then whatever it was, you had to haul it. You had to deliver it in those days.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Now even in our time, a couple of families made a living on that, right in Genesee. Oh yes. They'd been up and then...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Gilts.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: There was some Gilts. They had two drain lines.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, everybody didn't have a pickup truck. Everybody didn't have a one-tonner or anything of the kind. So if they wanted coal or anything else, somebody had to haul it to them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It's a plain fact that they couldn't get enough pieces of wool. There were some 24 wools in there. There were registered wools and all that. But there just wasn't enough good ones around. They wanted better ones and they couldn't get them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: To go back a little farther than your questioning went, Sam, our grandfather and father went to a purebred Hereford bull sale in Hamilton, I think it was.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The Grand.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Was it the Grand?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was in...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: that was in 96 or something.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I believe that's right.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And they bought, I think, three bulls and put them in the ranger's diameter. And to begin with, they were the laughing stock of the ranger's community. They were much smaller, looked smaller than the big, long-legged cattle. But at the end of the second year, when they began to have the saleable steers from those bulls, they found out that they weighed a great deal more than the other cattle a year older. And this kind of triggered a demand for Herefords. They introduced the Herefords into the ranger's cattle industry in the summer of the 19th century.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And this germinated the demand for them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So this was one of the many factors that kind of worked together to get my dad and his brother into the purebred cattle business 20 years later. 15 years, I guess. They were known as having introduced these bulls. They had the reputation of having the best ranger's cattle in the area where they operated. It was a chore to get enough good bulls. So it was a logical complement to their range of stuff. They started producing some purebred cattle of their own, to supply part of their own demand, all of their own demand, prior to other people's demand. And it made a logical combination of enterprises. They had this family farm, Gunnery, that they had to take over responsibility for operating because our grandfather had died in 1912. And I guess they rented the place out for a few years.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And didn't Kraut rent and farm the place for a while?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't think Kraut ever did, but he farmed it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Stuckert had it for a year or two. And Post had it for a couple of years.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know if there was anybody else.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Do you know of anybody else named?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, if they got back onto it in 1915, that would be about the limit. Unless someone read it and used it while Grandpa was still alive. No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember much about, know much about how the Salmon River operation was set up? What kind of an area they had and the seasonal work situation down there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I don't remember that very well.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, it was a typical range. Cattle out, but as far as this area is concerned, it's rough country. Very rough. Cheek grass, bunch grass. Not very much brush. So, pretty well watered. It's summered on the mountain. Be the same as if you come up from Lewis and it's summered here and meadows up here. Same thing. We had meadows there and timbers summered there. Raised enough hay on the river to winter the cattle by irrigating it. And of course it was grass-beaked. They didn't feed them, I think, at that time. They were usually sold to buyers from old, some of the packers in Spokane or Seattle or somewhere like that. Stanton and Frye or Swift.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The cattle were ordinarily sold right on the range, weren't they, to buyers who came from the North hidden part of the country?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Quite often. Quite often.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But those buyers, like John Bearer, for instance, he represented that Spokane opera. He was buying with their checkbook.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where on the Salmon River was the operation? Do you know where Winchester is?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It's been in Winchester for about 20 miles straight south. Just due south.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: In general, it was on both sides of the river from there to the north of the river.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That area was heavily used by number of ranchers in those days?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, there were lots of homesteaders in there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They were very late surveying that. They were either around 1909 or 1910 that they were surveyed out. And afterwards, after it became surveyed, the homesteaders just locked in there and took it all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was your father's place purchased or was it homestead?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was his homestead.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, there was... Well, he... Go ahead. No, you go. Well, there was some irrigated land later on this...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: on this Deer Creek place, wasn't there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, yes. There was...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know. They used to call it 20 acres. I question the 20. But that's what they called it. And it was very productive. It had never been really cropped, you see. It was virgin land. They put water on alfalfa and that kind of soil and it'll do pretty well. I don't know. He bought Wes's relinquishment on that. But it had never been surveyed at the time. So actually, he's the original entry on it. Couldn't say he bought Wes's relinquishment. It was Wes's spotter's right and Wes bought his from another fellow.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So... No one knew where they were... what they were taking up or where it was.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It's not... not... according to the surveys or anything like that. He just had a place there and if he was there and in possession, why nobody bought it, he... At that particular time, there was lots of land. But a few years later, it was gone. But of course, these homesteaders led this such steep country that they had no way on 160 to make a living. They just... Oh, spent the winter and quite part of the spring, they couldn't find a job on the place. They planted the garden and built a house and managed to prove up and then sold it. If they couldn't sell it to one of the stockmen, they mortgaged it to the bank and let the bank take it over.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That was it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: What about the old Deer Creek Mine there? Was it early days or wasn't it...?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The lower... the Deer Creek Mine was fairly early days. The Horseman Mine on top of the hill, which I...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, that's the one I was talking about. Well, I thought maybe it was.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But that came along just before the First World War.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
