speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That they started that. But the other one was... The other one was around 1900, on down below, at the fort where they had the big tunnel where they put in the mill down there. I don't know. That was a kind of a... It was kind of a typical Vince Leroy promotion. They did have considerable value in both those places, but it's just not concentrated enough that you can go in there and make it pay off. I don't know. With gold, the price it is now, and copper, maybe those mines could be profitably operated. If somebody wanted to take a chance on how long those prices would stay up.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That's funny, thank you.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you work down there much when you were a kid? On the place?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: All the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of work did you do?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, my dad bought me a saddle horse when I was five years old, and I've been a punching cows ever since. Until I hear four years ago, I had a stroke and I had to sell the ranch. That's a good...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He started riding it fine then, eh?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know how old he was when he used to ride at these rodeos, and thought he was making pretty good money getting five dollars a head for riding ponies out of the chute. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I'd like to know something that was like that when you were a kid working on the place. What kind of work you did.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, I did about everything. This little hay and fed a few cows with it. I did about everything you do on the saddle horse.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you starting to do some pretty man-sized work when you were just a kid then?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I don't know. My dad used to... I used to go up to my dad to the mountain and have to move the cattle out and he'd go off and leave me. It's around the place when I was nine, ten years old. So I guess I was doing what a man does.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh boy. Well, that was pretty good.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Tie together. You'd have to put the Salmon River and Genesee operations together.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how did they fit together?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, after the purebred cattle operation was set up, of course they were a natural complement to the extent that the Genesee ranch produced the herd bulls for the range operation. We never used that Genesee operation to provide feed for the range. Because that was an entirely different type of wintering. They were not entirely truthful there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Did they send some grain to gather from there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But in the beginning the cattle were brought... beef cattle were brought from the Salmon River and fed to Genesee.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, I didn't know about that.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Just before they were sold?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: They were sold as fed cattle rather than grass. Rather than grass cattle. This is in the beginning now when my grandfather was running the operation and my dad was just a kid to help me.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, was that some of the use that was made of the hay that Pop used to bale then when he was running the baling outfit?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I suspect he didn't bale very much plaid hay. I think he was in that for a few side dollars. That's what I thought. According to the book that I had on his operations there, I don't know whether you got that or whether I still got it down there, but... There's no plaid hay listed as being baled. It's other people around. Mostly out on the breaks on the reservation.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I didn't remember that thing about cattle ever being fed there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This must have been very early in the operation. In the 90s.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I think it was... I know part of it was when they had the butcher shop. That's something you didn't even know about, I suppose.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I can't think of the other Dutchman's name. He ran off with all of it. Oh yeah, Platten Bomberg.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Bomberg, yeah.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Platten Bomberg owned a butcher shop once. I can still remember Grandma one time getting the books out on that butcher shop operation. You'd be surprised how many people around Genesee who'd Platten Bomberg give a butcher bill that they never did pay.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: that butcher operation was pretty much cutting out the middle man then?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, it was, but it went broke anyway.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Probably everybody had their own.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, talking about Bomberg then, what was the guy's name that drowned down at the Clearwater that was with Eli at that time?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: He was the name something like that, but I don't know if that was it. The guy that drowned there at the railroad bridge.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, I know they used to pour that river there. I remember sitting on Watson's front porch and Eli telling him about that and describing it, but I don't know the name.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was it that happened on this guy Brown?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, he couldn't swim and they were taking cattle across the river and apparently his horse got in trouble. He didn't get off of him anyway. He was still sitting on him.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Down he went. Apparently the horse just fell down or went into a deep hole or something there, stepped into a hole, some kind of a hole. It was kind of a dangerous ford anyway.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This is... as I got the story, this was a heck of a big man anyway. The horse didn't even come up for a while.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I wanted to finish talking about the operation. You were sort of the middle of saying about how the two tied together, raising the bulls in Genesee.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Is there any more about that?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, actually it was so short-lived because of the intervention of the post-World War I depression that there wasn't much of a story to tell. It seemed to me a natural putting together of resources. They had the family farm in Genesee that needed to be used and was a logical place to raise purebred cattle because they needed a different kind of care. Supervised breeding, controlled feeding, used a lot of grain and so on that you didn't apply to a range setup. And then, of course, they still had the range setup and they supplied the bulls and perhaps occasionally they even weeded out cows from the purebred herd and shifted over to that herd to upgrade it. So it made a natural combination of resources. Also, there was the fact that my father and uncle each were fully competent of running either end of this. They didn't need both of them, they needed one, so they kind of divided the forces for that. So it was a natural outgrowth of enterprise. So it was a standard one.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that a pretty wild country when you were growing up there in the Salmon River?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I mean, I've heard some of the more wild west kind of tales of North Idaho coming out of that country.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Most of that sort of thing is made up, but it wasn't all made up. But it's a rough country, real steep. You don't go anywhere much there without a saddle horse. It's too hard walking. And there's no other way. You can fly over it with an airplane, but you can't land one there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Are there any incidents that come to your mind from the stories that they told in the early days?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, there were rough times. There were sheep men killed and horse thieves hung in one thing and another. Rather than do a man, Monty Jarrett, you get a scar that runs right across there. He said a rancher caught him stealing a horse one time, that's where the 30-30 creased even. He had to get away with the horse.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, we used to hear allegations of cattle rustling and horse stealing and so on. In our midst, I don't know how much of it was ever confirmed. It's one thing to miss a cow or a steer, another thing to find the myth in somebody else's possession. There was some of that going on.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I've heard the stories too about that country that somebody said one time about. A cowboy coming up there from Texas or down in that country. After about a month or so in that Salmon River country, he was all through the idea that lands are steep, that the cow couldn't even stay on the side of the hill. That wasn't his idea of a place to ride. Heard cows. Find someplace else to herd them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I guess this happened too quite regularly, didn't it, Tom?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Bad winter, they'd slip off the hillsides. Oh, you met a cow or a horse will slide there in that country. You go down there now, in some of those places I used to trot and run a saddle horse down. I wouldn't run nothing down there now. You couldn't pay me enough to run a saddle horse down some of those hills.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you get snowed in there for months at a time in the winter?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Sometimes.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Sometimes. See, they had to come over the hill by forest. Come out over the top of the Craig Mountain in order to get out of there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: At that time you could figure on about five feet of snow on Craig Mountain every winter. Unless there was a good deal of travel through and kept the trail packed. Well, you could get into a lot of trouble. Well, you could even then because it happened to warm up and begin to fall. A little horse slide off the trail and get bogged down in the snow on the side.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And there were years when they had lots more snow than that because I don't know if you'd remember it, Kenneth, but remember where the shop was at 8th place on the mountains there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Just outside. Well, maybe you remember there were some black pine trees there. Well, there used to be a lot more of those, I guess. But there was three or four stumps out in there. You take a horse about cave wire size and ride out there and just reach over and lay your hand on top of the stumps. They just got caught there one winter and that's where they sawed the trees down on top of the snow for wood. Right there, just about seven feet of snow.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, another index of the answer to your question, Sam, is that people who live down in the bottom of the San Pedro Canyon ordinarily pack in their winter supplies in the fall. And they expected to be holed up for three to five months before it was practically packed again.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember pretty well what you lived on in the way of food during the winter there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, I suppose I do. Well, we usually had plenty of homegrown spuds and quite a lot of canned vegetables. Bought some in cans. I guess most of what anybody else would live on.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Had your own beef?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Bacon and beef. You had hogs too.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, we didn't raise hogs. It wasn't very successful. It was a pack and grain 14 miles on a pack horse to raise hogs. It didn't work either way. You see, in 1919 there was a lot of grain over on Omak there. Oh, it's in that book. Bill, he bought a whole bunch of this wheat over there. And then bought feeder pigs and took them in there. And long in the wintertime they got ready for market. So we started driving out to Grangeville. We drove them up Whitewood and got over the hill down towards Toll Lake there. And they got them into a barn overnight. And when they went out the next morning it was zero weather. The damn pig was all piled in one corner. And only the ones on top was alive. So it wasn't a paying proposition.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, my recollection of what we ate included lots of beans and rice and macaroni and almost all kinds of dried fruits. We had relatives in California and we'd send there and get raisins and dried prunes in the wholesale lots. And the bacon, we bought in whole sides of course. And I suppose there was some salt pork and that sort of thing too at the time. Lots of cured and dried stuff that could be packed and kept without a storage box.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: See, there was no refrigeration in those days. People would live where they could cut ice. Of course they had ice boxes but out on a lone ranch there's not much chance of that. So you had to buy things that couldn't be stored.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the neighbors around you when you were on a ranch there? Did you see other people much, especially the winners?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, occasionally though. There was dancers in one thing or another.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: See the winners.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Kind of got them together. I suppose by today's standards you'd say you didn't see very much of each other, really.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: How far did Harry live from us?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Five miles. Five miles by saddle horse.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he a close neighbor?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, no, we had one neighbor a mile away. And as long as Ross was with us, stayed there. But he moved up and moved right out. We had one a mile away in each direction. Then each two directions.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I guess from the period from about 1910 to 1915, when the homesteads were mostly being taken up, and the country was mostly being filled up with young people, we had house warnings and weddings and that sort of thing. That fairly frequently. Those didn't take too much an excuse to get people to go somewhere.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, they kind of looked for an excuse to go somewhere, I think.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But there was no store or was there a school in there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Only was it our house.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Only private.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Just our family. Our father hired a teacher who lived in our house. There was one house warning. I remembered I didn't go to it because I was too small. My dad and mother went to a homestead cabin house warning a few miles up the river from us. My mother made a cake to take them on, and she also took along a kerosene lamp to light up the occasion. When they got there, they found the lamp that soaked out of the kerosene and soaked out of the lamp and the cake didn't make it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Did it was a teacher there for just a part of the year?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, I think the months that we were pulled up on the calendar. About five months, she taught there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That or closer to six. It was pretty standard, I guess. I know that as a seventh grader I came out to Genesee just a couple of weeks before the end of the term. I moved in seventh grade and passed the examination there with no problem. So I think it was, I think what was taught was pretty standard stuff that teachers would all have their certificates.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have a number of different teachers through the years? Or would the same person come back?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Four. Four years. We had one teacher, two different terms. The others were all just one term.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it very hard on you as far as making you stick to the grindstone instead of being in a classroom with a lot of kids? I wonder whether you...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, as I recall, we observed school hours pretty closely. School was always an adventure to me, so it was never a hardship. I wasn't even aware that school was supposed to be hard. I don't know how the others reacted.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, there probably wasn't much you could have done that time of year anyway outside, so you probably would have been in anyway.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how many of you were there then, the kids, going to school?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I guess five was the most... Our youngest sister was just barely old enough to start school.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Tom, you had a couple years of Genesee before that started, didn't you?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Three years, I think. I wouldn't swear to it anymore. I think it was three years ago.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: You stayed at Grandma Platt then and went to school. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you tell about the bad winter again and what that was like when it was so hard on the cattle after the war? What winter was that?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: 1919 and 1920, they said.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was it that happened?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, it was just a winter with a lot of snow and a lot of cold and short feet. That particular area just didn't have any feet in there. Cold was an extremely dry, cold summer, and the grass never grew very well. So when it came time to put cattle in the feedlot, they just didn't have enough feet. Eventually the 700 head ended up down at the top of this, the feedlot's down there. Well, on numbers that would indicate that they were something like 60 % short of feet. And it was cold enough that they drove those 700 cattle across salmon over on the ice, which is getting pretty cold if you've seen the salmon right now because it's a pretty fast turbine in the stream. One of them went to take them out there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: As I remember the story that at the time they said that they started feeding, well, John says in this that they started feeding cattle there, feeding these 700 head of cattle $7 a ton of hay, and before they got through it was $50 a ton. But the thing I remembered was that the price of beef was about $36 when they went there, but it was only $9 in the next spring after they fed them all winter, brought them through the winter. So they had to bring part of them back home. There wasn't anything they could do with it. They did sell quite a few of them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, a cow that consistently stays that cold unless she's awfully well fed, she just won't hold her own or do any good. And of course it stayed cold way late in the spring, and so they lost a lot of calves. Cows were in such poor condition that they didn't breed back good. And the next year's calf crop wasn't any good. And a thing like that carries on for several years, you see.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You were saying that the tits were so cold that they froze?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, cows that were sucking calves, the calves would suck me, the cows' tits wet, and then it was so cold that it would freeze.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It would drop off.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It destroyed the udders.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I think the remarkable thing about this whole thing, though, was the way that Bill and John, after they had gone through this, had everything put up for sale. And John took 350 head of gum or ewes, ewes that wouldn't sell anyway, the old ones. Bill took 16 or 17 head of bread, Hereford heifers, and they went their own way. And within two or three years, John was a sheep man and had a band of sheep, and Bill was back in the cattle business. And this to me is the remarkable thing that cattlemen or stockmen can just sit back and wait for nature to take its course, and the increase will come if they can wait long enough. If you can find some way to eat while you're gone, you can do it. That probably was part of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How would you recall just what that post-war depression meant around this area for farmers that had a hard time?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I wouldn't say that farmers generally had a hard time. The price a week stayed reasonably good. It wasn't like it was in the time. It wasn't too many years until it was a dollar and a quarter, a dollar and a half, around there. It was because of the shortage of hay in certain areas, well, in fact, on large areas that hurt the stockmen. The one that sold his beef during the summer when he could have got a good price for it instead of holding it for a higher price, he didn't do too bad. And a lot of farmers would cry about that because they could have sold their wheat for $1 .45 or $2 .45 and was going to have two and a half. And eventually they took a dollar and a quarter for it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But why did the bottom fall out of the cattle market?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I wouldn't for sure know. Just that the war was over and maybe there was little more meat around than needed or something. The government quit buying tremendous amounts of it, you should see, when they brought a couple of million men home from France and quit having to ship that stuff over there to feed them, or they just didn't buy anymore.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This came quite a little while before the start of the real depression thing came, too. This was ten years before. If this came in 1920, say, or shortly after that, the farmers were still enjoying pretty fair prices through 1929 at least. Then they began to get the pinch. As Tom said, some of them took a dollar and a quarter. I've had them tell me they took 35 cents. Some of them as low as 17 cents a bushel.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What time?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: In the early 30s then.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, so far as the late tall county farmers are concerned, the depression in the 30s was far, far worse than the other. No question about that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But to the ranchers, would you say the earlier one was as severe?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, don't you suppose this came from, as Tom said, from a poor grass crop, a poor crop of hay, and having all this stock that had to be fed. Well, this just naturally threw these fellows into a depression. Maybe it wasn't wide, although it must have been wide, too, because if they said that they could have got 36 cents for their beef when they took it down there and could only get nine cents when they got ready to move it out of there, beef must have been dropping pretty fast over winter.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, after that war, it was the fact that a lot of the industry shut down, too. There was a good deal of unemployment and there wasn't the money around to buy high-priced stuff that had been there a short while before.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: There was a different cause of difficulty in Latah County among the folks who were strict with farmers, and that is that during the last years of World War I, the price of wheat got up to two and a half bushel, maybe somewhat higher, and this touched off a lot of land buying speculation. Land in the Genesee area that had been worth maybe $75 an acre before the war was selling for $200, $250 an acre. And people who bought that land and went out on the limb without enough money and the paperwork were caught. Then in the depression after the war, there were low crop prices that wouldn't pay for land valued that high, and some of those folks had to give up. They lost their farms and their farms were combined. This was kind of the beginning of combining farms into bigger patches. Folks that had big enough areas and were well enough financed to stay with it bought up some of these farms that had to be abandoned because of bankruptcy.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: There were speculators, too. For instance, in the early days here, this man Williamson that had a store here in Moscow wasn't a speculator. His son is my neighbor now. Frank told me that he always worked on the idea that once he had enough of a hole on a ranch that he could borrow some money on it, he'd go out and put it down on something else. Well, when he got all through, Frank ended up by having just one 160-acre ranch over at Pullman that he could save out of all of these dead heads. And the Toomey place down in Genesee was one of them that he had at one time. He just kept buying every time he got a foothold on a piece of land and could borrow some more money, then he'd go out and buy something else. And if times would have kept going up, he'd have been all right, but they didn't.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: What I wonder about now, aren't we in the same kind of a thing right now?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: You're talking, Kenny, about prices going from $75 to $200 or $250 or something. Now they tell me that some of our farmland is selling as high as $850 an acre. No one can make that kind of money from that piece of land if they depend on the piece of land to make the money. That's right.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: And it isn't farmers that are offering that kind of money. It's people who have other income, people who have industrial income or some other enterprise against which they can take a loss on the farm and take a tax credit for it. I was told by Rudolph Norby the last time I talked to him that one of his neighbors was offered $1 ,200 an acre for 1 ,000 acres of land toward Uniontown. This was not an offer made by another farmer. It was an offer made by a California investor who perhaps has an industrial development for some other business against which he can take credit in the tax write-off on that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would his long-range interest be in owning land that cost him that much? Would he be able to do it?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, under our present income tax setup, he can take off any loss that...if he can show a loss on this farm that it isn't paying out, he can take this directly out of his profits from the other organization, whatever he has. So until they straighten up this kind of a thing, there will always be some of that going on. But I know Kenny in one or two cases where it has been the farmer who bought the land, but it was land that joined him and he could farm it without any additional equipment and he probably had the money to buy it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: In this circumstance, it makes some sense. Talking about speculation, they say that a lot of places, I guess, had certain amounts of speculation in the pioneering days, some more than others. Some places had boosters coming in, guys that were just trying to take advantage of the fact that the land was just opening up, even planning to stay there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know how much of an idea, how much of that there was around Genesee and how much of it, as opposed to how the people just coming in to buy and sell for the amount they could?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, from what I can remember, I would say that most of the people who came in there came in with the idea of staying because the valley to the north was Scandinavian, the valley to the west was German, and they just kind of came and landed in communities and they built their homes and built a church. I don't think there was very little speculation. The place where there might have been a little speculation early would have been like this town of Blaine, which isn't even here anymore, just over the Paradise Hill. It used to be on the old Genesee to Moscow Road, and there was a sawmill and a grocery store and a church and a school, cut quite a little timber right in there, but now it's all farmland. It's all been cleared and it's all open to farmland. There might have been some speculation in places like that. That speculation was probably on the town mostly, I would think, that there might be a town there that would be something.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I think that's true, and that was a phase which passed very early. It was part of the original tide of land settlement and early development. Before the railroads came, there was always an uncertainty of where the railroad would be when it did come, and so there was speculation on that. You can read the history of the railroads in Mato County and adjoining Prickman County and find that half a dozen towns thought they were going to be the capital of the state one of these days because the railroad was going to come there first, but it didn't. It went somewhere else. A lot of these little towns just stabilized at a much lower level or some of them disappeared almost entirely. They didn't get a permanent set up to back up their means. In the first 10 or 20 years of a lot of pioneer communities, from what I've read, there was a great deal of turnover. They've been trying to do some statistical research. They find that 70, 80 percent of the people would not stay from one census to the next, which is the only measure they've got.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that around Genesee there was unusual stability?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yes, I do. I think Dave has the right idea there. The people that came to settle most of that country came intending to stay. They came from harder circumstances than they came to, even though this was a pioneer country. The Scandinavian people and German people who came in here came from much more difficult climates and limited land resources, limited opportunities. They had no way to go but up when they got to a good farming country where they had their own land and all they had to do was persevere. That's pretty much how it went. It's a commonplace of land development in most areas that it takes about three generations of investment before the land actually pays back enough to pay off the last investment. This has been true of virtually all of the irrigation projects in Idaho, for example. A new irrigation project has opened up. People move in and host at the land. They spend all of their resources in developing as much of the land as they can. They find they can't make a living so they sell out to somebody else, ordinarily taking considerable loss on their investment up to that point. The next developer puts in his investment and develops some more land. He can't make a go of it. Finally the third investor comes along and by that time enough of the previous investment has been written off in the price that he pays and enough improvement has been made in the resource that he can make a living. From there on things stabilize.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The third one has probably got a bigger ranch. He's probably got two ranches or more by that time. I think this is true. I think this is true in the irrigated country, in the big band and all that country, even with government help. I don't know if this goes so much that way but I think of the Genesee country now. You fellas remember young Qualley Ernest Qualley down there. His dad raised a family, I don't know how big a family, on eighty acres. When he went to work he started farming while he had to have two or three times that much. Now his son is farming on I don't know what size his ranch is but I suppose eight hundred acres or seven hundred acres like all the rest of them down there to make a living. But still his dad raised a family on eighty acres.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This is part of the explanation or at least relates to the explanation of why farmers can pay seemingly impossible prices now for additional farmland. You usually find that the farmer who pays such a high price already has a substantial growing outfit. And if he's a third generation farmer like the Qualley grandson who is now farming in the Genesee area, he has pretty much inherited what he has. It's almost a free asset. So if he has a thousand acres for which he paid nothing, as we say, he can buy another hundred and sixty acres to average in with that at a very high price and his overall cost of land is still a reasonable figure. This same man, if he had to go to the bank and borrow the money and buy that land and pay for it to pay off a loan covering the old value of the land, he couldn't possibly make it. He has to average in some other assets that cost much less.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I always think that way about old Charlie Funkhouser over there who was a banker at Palouse for many years. He owned a couple hundred acres out there and he always claimed that Palouse land was only worth sixty-seven dollars an acre. When he had time to sell his, he'd get two hundred or two and a quarter for it. But probably as far as the bank was concerned, sixty-seven would have been the figure they'd started using. That had been the amount they'd loaned on it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I was thinking about the post-World War I tough winter again and I was just wondering about the effects on that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it across the board for what it did in the country around here?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I'd say it was on livestock anyway, sheep and cattle anyway. I don't suppose it affected the hogs very much because wintertime hogs are locked up anyway.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It must have affected the labor market though because I ran a camp, NRA, which was National Resource Act, I believe, Recovery Act. They paid those boys sixty cents an hour I think and a dollar an hour for cooks and so forth. But they had plenty of takers and that was something on the order of the CC except that they were just working for wages. So I would imagine there was plenty of labor force that was looking for work.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: What year was that?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was in... 34.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, no, what I was talking about was the 19...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: we're skipping around. Oh, okay. You're still talking about over 19, 1920 and so forth. You said that year the horses' tails got stuck.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Cows' tails froze down at night, see, when they lay down. And when they get up they just pull their hair out of their tails. Well... There's cows all over the country without any bush on their tails next spring.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: There wasn't any...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Yeah, on the bed grounds, you know, boy, they'd tuck their tail between their legs and the heat on the body would melt them down in. But during the night it gets cold and freeze up again. And I remember Bill Platt coming out here and telling us it was so damn cold that they had cows laying down on the bed ground but froze down. They couldn't get up. Right on the bed ground in the feedlot. And these were well-fed cattle he was talking about, reasonably well-fed. They had to go around in the morning and rake them loose.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So they could stand up. I don't think wages were very good for some time after this 20 thing. Because I can remember working at the Genesee Union warehouse for a couple of years and I'm sure I worked for about 60 cents an hour or something of the kind working in the warehouse. And before that and after that wages went up some in price. Although maybe not so awfully high.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: By the time I was working for wages out in harvest in the middle 20s, two bits an hour was the harvest wage. Four dollars a day for a 12 hour day. So wages were awfully cheap.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Thinking along that same line, I worked for Bunker Hill and Sullivan for six months in the mine. And that was either in 20 or 21 and I got four and a quarter a day for that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Eight hours?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Eight hours. So the wages weren't anything outstanding.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: You didn't have very much of the time you paid for your bed and your rooms. No.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Paid for your room and the board and so forth. I forgot now what it cost. It couldn't have been more than $30 a month or so.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you find on the operation that you could keep your health pretty well?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, I don't know. We had quite a few incompetent people out there at the ranch at different times. Kids that came out of Spokane and one thing or another. Take them out to pitch hay. It was just about as well pitched as yourself because you had a long bed. They never had a pitchfork in their hands before.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: You know what to do with it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: But no, by and large now I don't think Bill had any trouble on Salmon River. He had experienced men there all the time. But there were homesteaders from around there that had been there a while and knew something about the country. They were looking for a few dollars. Yeah. He didn't have any trouble there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I think that by and large all through that period up until after the 1930s depression, the labor market was largely a buyer's market even on ranches. There were some men who were pretty picky and choosy about where they worked and how much they got paid. But you could nearly always find men who were looking for work. There was a great deal of itinerant labor needed in the blues country then because the harvesting piled up, the grain was bound rather than combined. And harvesting required a lot of extra help to manage the horses and pitch the bundles and thrash the grain and so on. And there was quite a lot needed in haying time. There was a lot of seasonal work. With the high-powered tractors now and self-propelled combines, they do up this work in 30 days. It used to take a much longer time with horsepower and hand power and with a lot fewer people to do it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I tell the story, Kenny, about the... And all in the world that that outfit owned was a tent for a cookhouse and a tent to cover the horses and some horses and plows or a couple plows and the Fresnos. That's the way they built that Genesee Highway to start with. And it's still in the same place that it was built then, although they've come in since then and cut one or two of the hills down a little more. But then they went on from that and then went off down that Boise country. And during the World War or during the Second War or something, they became another Morris Knutson and went all over the world building airfields and so forth.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This is the Turley outfit?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Mm-hmm, Turley Brothers. They started here in Moscow. In fact, there's one of them living at Boise now. Well, there may be more than one of them, but there's one of the grandsons living at Boise now, they tell me, that has a big ranch out there and he's collecting old threshing machines and old sawmills or anything of this kind that the next generation would be interested in. And he's making it into a kind of an amusement park thing, take children out to look, let them see how things went on in the good days, if that's what you call them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you have to cross the Salmon at other times with cattle? I mean, was river crossing part of the operation?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, at times when it had to be. But cattle, that's too big a river, cattle won't cross that unless you request their force to it, of course. But in our time, there were no bridges. And a beef cut being taken from Joseph Mountain on the other side of the river had to be swum across. There was no other way.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I did have a ferry, I used the ice-crake and that whiteboard, but there was no corrals or anything leading on to it. So there was no way to get loose cattle on there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you make cattle cross yourself?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I've helped swim cattle at Salmon many times.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's it like?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh, you just take a small bunch that you can be sure to handle, maybe seven or eight or ten head. And decide where you're going to put them in. And two or three fellows, a couple behind and one on each side, you start them on the run down the river and they'll go in. If you can keep that lead bunch headed across, the others will go fairly easy.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Cattle will follow the river.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The early day people and maybe still some of them do occasionally swim, they swim cattle across the snake too.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Tom, did you ever see the techniques used of putting a young calf in the back of a rowboat and coaxing the mother in?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: No, but I coaxed the whole herd up the highway.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Not in the rowboat, but with a calf in a pickup. Darn right.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Put a calf in the pickup and let them all find out exactly where he is. You've got to lead them right up the highway. Take the whole bunch and just go.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, it's the technique as old as time, as I've seen in the old tomb inscriptions in Egypt. The hieroglyphic inscriptions there, a picture of a boat crossing a body of water with a calf bawling out of the back end, and the mother bawling out in the swimming water. I suppose they were taken across the Nile.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Probably were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I'd like to ask you a little bit about what you remember about the World War I years in the Genesee area. How the local people reacted to the war being on and what effect that had and what people did.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I saw it of course with very young eyes because I was only ten years old in 1917 when we moved to the Genesee country from the Salmon River. But I remember this period of great dedication on the part of everybody. In school we knit mittens and we sewed this and that and so on for the soldiers. We saved prune pits because they took the nuts out of those and extracted something that was used to make gas masks. We saved all kinds of stuff. Tin flour, I remember, was something we were supposed to save. And there was great enthusiasm whenever there was a bond sale or any kind of a money raising deal. I remember we had an old rooster that must have been, I suppose, about a ten pounder. It was a great big Plymouth Rock and old this time. And my dad took him to an auction sale and he was sold several times at this sale. Nobody wanted to keep him so they'd buy him and put him back in the sale and my dad finally came home with him. But that one rooster raised fifteen or twenty dollars and he was sold over and over again.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Incidentally, they used the shell, the nutshell, the shell of your prune pits or anything like that. That was transformed into charcoal for the gas masks.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That's what they used. Well, one thing I knew about it was that there was an Idaho company down on the Mexican border before this thing started. They were training down there and they were called into active duty and then taken down and guard the railroads and this type of thing before they finally went into this western outfit that went overseas anyway. So there were quite a few boys from the Genesee area that were in active duty over there. Kenny says he was about ten years old. I was seventeen, or would have been seventeen at the end of 1917. So I was just about to the age where I could have gotten in when the thing ended.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember there being much concern locally about the IWWs?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Okay, I'll tell you a story now. I was working for the IWWs, had been in full swing anyway for some little time, and I was working for an outfit. Jones, Frank Jones was one of them. I can't even tell you the other guy's name now, but anyway, it was two partners on this thrashing machine. We pulled into a field and we were thrashing loose oats and the wind was coming just the wrong way. It was coming right back at our face. I went in once and unloaded and came out choking to death. So when I went out in the field then to load up again with a wagon, I came back in and I told these fellows, I said, I'm not going back in there anymore. That isn't any place for a guy to be at all. Unless you want to turn this machine around, I'm just going to unhook. Some of your other fellows are going to quit you too because they're all grumbling about it. Well, that was the wrong thing to say because right away they said, well, we'll just take you to town then for IWW. I told them, I told you, I told you. This was Frank Jones and the other fellow that was there, he just kind of laughed about it and he wrote out my check and offered me a ride to town anyway. But Frank was all for taking me into Moscow anyway and I was one of the strike leaders. But I would have been all right if I'd just told him I was going to quit. But I was through. When I told him the rest of them didn't like it, they were all going to quit. That was taking her a little too far, I guess.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I've heard rumors about suspected sabotage that the IWW did in the farming country. But what I've heard from old loggers is pretty much along the lines that they don't believe that they actually did much in that period of time in the farming country. I was wondering what...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The idea was that they were supposed to have fed boxes of matches or something of this kind into the separators. And the separators blew up from smut explosions. But then how many of them were just smut explosions and how many of them had something to do with somebody setting them off, I don't have any idea.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I think there were two or three sizable grain fires in the big van that they figured was set. They were set.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Who set them?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That's something else again. They never did prove who did it.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't think they figured it out too much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was smut a big problem during that time? Were smut fires real dangers? I mean, a real possibility around Genesee?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Oh yeah, always. They didn't have the smut resistant to varieties and smut was much more common. I was involved in the smut explosion in the threshing crew that I worked with one year. I was the last wagon unloading at the end of the day when you scoop up the accumulated stuff off the bottom of the rack. It just shattered out in your bundle rack through the day. And this included a lot of dust and smut. I didn't know that anybody did. The machine exploded while I was unloading. But the operator was all race for it. It was a smutty field and he was operating a steam powered outfit. He had a steam line from this boiler right into the separator. And when that machine blew, the engineer revved up the engine, turned the steam into the separator. The separator tender was up on the top of that separator in a flash. He wasn't there already and he cranked the straw blower away from the straw stack. They blew the fire right out of that machine. It was out in less than five minutes. It blew a big hunk of flaming straw out onto the edge of the straw stack. But there were half a dozen guys standing around there and they got in with their pitchforks and shuffled that away from the straw stack. It burned a piece of stubble maybe half the size of this house and in a few minutes it was all over with. They replaced some burned out straw racks in the machine that night and the next morning we started off on time. But I think this is probably no different from most smut explosions of that time. They didn't have to be set. The operators were taking every possible precaution to avoid an explosion and be ready for it if it did occur. This is the way that one was handled.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did the smut problem start in the teens or was it something that was there from the beginning? Do you know?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I don't know, but I presume that we always had it from the time we got a week into the country.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Especially in a very few years, especially ...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The smut spore gets onto the healthy wheat kernel, you see, and is carried wherever the wheat goes. If you import the seed from an area where smut is common, you'd have smut with it. Then when you plant the seed, the smut germinates along with the wheat and grows right in the wheat kernel. It comes up through the stem of the wheat as a parasite and invades the new head and takes over the kernels there. It just multiplies until it completely replaces the normal vegetation there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I wonder how much of a problem that was, Kenny, though, in the early days when they used more hitters. They didn't have their bundles and so forth, but they headed the wheat and put it right into the machine.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Do you suppose this reduced the smut possibility a little?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know how it could have any effect. Well, I was thinking it might be a little more moist by still being standing wheat.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, when the wheat was headed that early, it was stacked and ripened in the stack rather than going direct into the machine.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I worked on one of the last header outfits that Shurmall had out there, the old header box for it, just for a short time. That was going directly into a machine.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, he hadn't given it right wheat. But one of the reasons the header went out and other systems came back in was that they could not wait until the wheat was ripe. By the time they got around to the last bit of wheat, it was shattering badly.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: On account of wind.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard all over the eastern part of the county, from Park, Erie, Troy, that in the early days people used to come to Genesee for the harvest from there. That was just a regular part of the work when they were homesteading out in that Troy area. So I get the idea that the harvest was really quite a big time for the whole county centered around Genesee in the early days.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well, I think this last outfit I worked on down there had something like 16 wagons. So that would have been 16 wagons there plus four pitchers in the field, plus a separator tender and the guy hauling water and the cooks and the engine man and all this type of thing. There probably were 30 people, 25 to 30 people mixed up in this operation. And this would go on for 30 to 35 days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were these owned by an individual or were they owned by individuals?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: By individuals mostly. This one that I was telling you about that I worked on, one of them that I worked on was this Costner and Jones. And then I remember another one, old Flamo. He ran there for years. That's all he did was just run the striation outfit in the summertime...

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It was a big business, the time you got all these men together and then by the time the farmer fed all these horses, out of the stock that was out there, out of the grain that was there. So this took an enormous amount of grain to keep the outfit going too. You asked something about wheat here. Up until the first war there at Genesee, wheat wasn't really such a big business probably because none of those flats up through there were even in wheat. They were all either in hay or pasture, one or the other. The hills were raising grain alright. Then it was after the start of this first world war that they finally decided they could raise wheat on those flats. So now it's strictly a wheat country.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You were talking about the weather changing and that's a common thing that climates changed around this county, this country.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you have any ideas about anything that people would say, used to say about why it changed, how it changed? I mean I know it changed by getting more money than it did, but what's the speculation on that? Did it change because the timber line moved back? Does that make a difference?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't know. Well of course the timber line has moved back. It used to be timbered clear down there around Blaine and in there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: What about there?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: This weather change seems to be a worldwide phenomenon. I've seen articles recently about this and what effect it may have over the long-forge and so on. I certainly recollect the much harder winters when we were kids and I encountered them.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Of course one thing about these county too is they didn't have any equipment for moving snow. So wherever it fell that's just where it stayed. They just tromped it down and left it right there. Or now they'll come along with motorized equipment and they'll knock it all off the highway and put it over on the edge of the road.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well when people started growing wheat in flats, is it because they thought the winters were getting milder? Were they just experimenting? Do you know how that development came about?

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well I would venture a couple of guesses. One, it sort of coincided with the high price of wheat during World War I. It was worth taking a flyer to plow some pasture and let it own and try to grow some wheat. Another guess would be that probably more winter hardy or frost resistant varieties had been developed by the experiment stations up to that time. They had previous ones.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: That may go find their rescue.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: So I think it was probably a natural change. And then of course once the tractors started coming in they didn't need all that metal and hay ground. They had to find something else to put on. It was the natural thing. We always had lots of livestock feed and so we raised feed crops on our flat ground. We had clover and grass mixtures on some of it. We raised summer crops, corn or sunflower, something like that, on some of the other. But I think that's probably an explanation of the change. There has been, I'm convinced, some change of climate. Some of these other changes would have occurred whether it was climate change or not in my opinion.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The change has reduced the water level around Genesee considerably. I don't know if you know about it, but Rudolph has got a shallow well out there back at the barn. A pitcher pump in it and a small trough. When he was using horses and milking cows there he just by hand pumped water for his livestock. And he had all the water he wanted. Now he can pump it dry in a few minutes.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: It's gone down that much.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Of course that's just a shallow thing, but still the water is just plain lower there even on the flats.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: Well I would guess that that again is a result of the combination of factors. When we used to summer fowl half the land, there was only crop there every year. And every year there would be crop there with new moisture. So now we crop every year. If it isn't wheat, it's peas or barley or lentils or something else. Every year there's crop on the ground and crops transpire tremendous amounts of water. When half the ground was summer fowl there was a chance for some of that water to go on down and add to the groundwater. Very little of it gets there I think. I hear you stirring about getting along. There's one area we haven't talked about at all that I would like to ask you to give some general impressions on. That is the different cultural groups that were around Genesee. And if there are any recollections you have of some of the early differences in ways between the Germans in the Norwegian and other groups that were there.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: I don't remember much about the early days because I didn't have much contact probably with those people. The Germans and the Catholics were pretty much west of town. The Scandinavians were north of town, pretty much in one valley. But when I was working with the CC boys all along the late 30s, I found that these Scandinavians, anyway, you never could go to their house without having cookies and coffee and so forth. They just had it for themselves there and anybody that came in had to stop and eat with them. That's all there was to it. They had to at least have coffee and cookies. But I think they were people who were kind of clannish, but still they were all progressive and they all worked in the community. I don't think they were clannish to the place where they wouldn't associate with anyone else.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
words: The need for interchange of labor and harvest, I think, pretty well bridged whatever cultural gap there might be. You need to work together in a pioneer situation.

speaker: Dave Hickman or Tom Platt or Kenneth Platt
